title: 1 Kings 11:26–43
context: Jeroboam, an able Ephraimite official, is met by the prophet Ahijah, who tears his new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten, announcing that God will give him ten tribes because of Solomon’s idolatry, while leaving one tribe for David’s sake. The promise to Jeroboam is conditional on obedience (11:38). Solomon seeks to kill him, and he flees to Egypt. Solomon dies after forty years. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about judgment, covenant faithfulness, and conditional promise.

verses.text: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother’s name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite and Solomon’s servant, whose mother Zeruah was a widow, rebels against the king. A third adversary appears.

Arminian readers see a capable man stepping into a role God will offer him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeroboam is introduced with his family and origin. The note about his widowed mother may underline his humble beginnings.

Reformed readers see God choosing an unlikely servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without assuming more about Jeroboam’s background than the text gives.

verses.text: This was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king: Solomon built Millo, and repaired the breach of his father David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason for his rebellion is connected with Solomon’s building of the Millo and repairing David’s city. The context is royal labor.

Arminian readers see grievances arising from heavy work demands.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator links the rebellion to building projects. Their exact connection is not spelled out.

Reformed readers see the setting for later complaints about the heavy yoke (12:4). Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without asserting details the text leaves implicit.

verses.text: The man Jeroboam was a mighty man of valor; and Solomon saw that the young man was industrious, and he put him in charge of all the labor of the house of Joseph.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam is a capable warrior, and Solomon puts him over the forced labor of Joseph’s tribes. He rises through ability.

Arminian readers see diligence rewarded and opportunity given. Faithful work in small things leads to larger responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Solomon recognizes Jeroboam’s skill and promotes him. The appointment places him among the northern tribes.

Reformed readers see providence positioning Jeroboam for his future role. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note how his position gives him influence among the people of Ephraim and Manasseh.

verses.text: At that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the way. Now Ahijah had clad himself with a new garment; and the two of them were alone in the field.
verses.arminianNotes:
As Jeroboam leaves Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh meets him in the field, wearing a new garment. The two are alone.

Arminian readers see God taking initiative through a prophet.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shiloh was once the site of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:3). A prophet from there now announces change.

Reformed readers see God’s word guiding history. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the private setting for a public prophecy.

verses.text: Ahijah took the new garment that was on him, and tore it in twelve pieces.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahijah tears his new garment into twelve pieces. The action is a living picture.

Arminian readers see prophetic symbolism making God’s message vivid and memorable. The torn cloth makes the coming division impossible to forget.
verses.reformedNotes:
The torn garment echoes Saul’s torn robe in 1 Samuel 15:27–28. Tearing signifies the kingdom’s division.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment dramatized. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about prophetic signs and the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: He said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces; for the LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon and will give ten tribes to you
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahijah tells Jeroboam to take ten pieces, for God will tear the kingdom from Solomon and give him ten tribes. The message is explicit.

Arminian readers see God offering Jeroboam a real opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes:
God himself will give the tribes. Jeroboam’s rise is God’s doing.

Reformed readers see God sovereignly distributing kingdoms. Both traditions read this as shared ground, affirming that God raises up rulers while those rulers remain responsible for how they respond.

verses.text: (but he shall have one tribe, for my servant David’s sake and for Jerusalem’s sake, the city which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel),
verses.arminianNotes:
One tribe will remain for David’s and Jerusalem’s sake, the city God chose. The promise to David stands.

Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness tempering judgment. Judgment is real, but it is not the last word for David’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jerusalem’s chosen status is reaffirmed. The Davidic line will not be extinguished.

Reformed readers see God’s covenant with David continuing. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the reckoning of tribes is not explained in detail, so interpreters account for it differently.

verses.text: because they have forsaken me, and have worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon. They have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in my eyes, and to keep my statutes and my ordinances, as David his father did.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason is that they have forsaken God and worshiped Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom, not walking in his ways as David did. Idolatry is the cause.

Arminian readers see judgment linked directly to chosen apostasy.
verses.reformedNotes:
The plural ‘they’ may include Solomon and the people with him. The sins named are the gods of 11:5–7.

Reformed readers see idolatry as the root offense. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s judgment on turning to other gods.

verses.text: “ ‘However, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him prince all the days of his life for David my servant’s sake whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes,
verses.arminianNotes:
God will not take the whole kingdom from Solomon, but will keep him as ruler for David’s sake. Mercy continues.

Arminian readers see God honoring David’s faithfulness through restraint. Even in judgment, God remembers his promises.
verses.reformedNotes:
David is described as one who kept God’s commandments, despite his own failures. The focus is his loyalty in worship.

Reformed readers see God’s mercy flowing from his covenant. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to promises made long before.

verses.text: but I will take the kingdom out of his son’s hand and will give it to you, even ten tribes.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will take the kingdom from Solomon’s son and give ten tribes to Jeroboam. The timing is set.

Arminian readers see judgment falling in the next generation as announced in 11:12.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise is repeated for emphasis. The transfer will happen after Solomon.

Reformed readers see God’s word certain to be fulfilled. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note that 12:15 later presents the division as fulfilling Ahijah’s word.

verses.text: I will give one tribe to his son, that David my servant may have a lamp always before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen for myself to put my name there.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will give one tribe to Solomon’s son so that David may always have a lamp before God in Jerusalem. The lamp signals continuity.

Arminian readers see hope preserved in the Davidic line.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ‘lamp’ image recurs in Kings (compare 15:4; 2 Kings 8:19). It speaks of an enduring Davidic presence.

Reformed readers see God keeping his covenant promise. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and Christians see it fulfilled ultimately in Christ, the son of David.

verses.text: I will take you, and you shall reign according to all that your soul desires, and shall be king over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will take Jeroboam, and he will reign over Israel according to all his soul desires. His kingship is God’s gift.

Arminian readers see a genuine calling offered to Jeroboam.
verses.reformedNotes:
God promises Jeroboam the throne. The offer is generous.

Reformed readers see God raising up a king by his sovereign choice. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the gift carries the conditions stated in the next verse.

verses.text: It shall be, if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do that which is right in my eyes, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, that I will be with you, and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and will give Israel to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
If Jeroboam listens to God and walks in his ways as David did, God will be with him and build him a sure house. The promise is conditional.

Arminian readers see covenant blessing tied to faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise parallels God’s covenant with David. It depends on Jeroboam’s obedience.

Reformed readers likewise affirm the real conditionality of this promise within its historical covenant setting. Both traditions read this as shared ground; Jeroboam’s failure to meet the condition will be shown in 12:25–33.

verses.text: I will afflict the offspring of David for this, but not forever.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
God will afflict David’s descendants for this, but not forever. Judgment has limits.

Arminian readers see hope for David’s line even in discipline. Discipline is meant to correct, not to destroy forever.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘Not forever’ points beyond the division. God’s purposes for David continue.

Reformed readers see a promise that Christians connect with the messianic hope. Both traditions read this as shared ground, cautiously, without claiming that the verse explicitly foretells a specific future event.

verses.text: Therefore Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon seeks to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam flees to Shishak king of Egypt and stays until Solomon’s death. The king resists God’s word.

Arminian readers see Solomon opposing God’s announced plan, as Saul once pursued David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Solomon’s attempt echoes Saul’s pursuit of David. Egypt shelters Jeroboam as it sheltered Hadad.

Reformed readers see God protecting the one he has chosen. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that Shishak appears again in 14:25.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, aren’t they written in the book of the acts of Solomon?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Solomon’s acts and wisdom are written in the book of the acts of Solomon. The narrator cites a source.

Arminian readers see the narrative pointing to a fuller record beyond what is included here.
verses.reformedNotes:
The book mentioned is not otherwise known to us. The narrator selects what serves his purpose.

Reformed readers see Scripture drawing on historical records. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without making claims about the cited source that the text does not support.

verses.text: The time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. His reign is summarized.

Arminian readers see a long reign whose ending is overshadowed by apostasy. Length of reign does not guarantee a faithful finish.
verses.reformedNotes:
The figure matches David’s reign (2:11). Some see it as a round number, others as exact; the text does not say.

Reformed readers see God’s patience over many years. Both traditions read this as shared ground and remember both Solomon’s great gifts and his tragic decline.

verses.text: Solomon slept with his fathers, and was buried in his father David’s city; and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon dies, is buried in David’s city, and Rehoboam his son reigns. The transition sets up chapter 12.

Arminian readers see the consequences of Solomon’s choices passing to his son.
verses.reformedNotes:
The burial formula closes Solomon’s story. The announced judgment now awaits Rehoboam.

Reformed readers see God’s word moving toward fulfillment. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the stage set for the division foretold by Ahijah.
